claude.sample_unit: clinical scenarios (3234 LLM responses vs 448 human responses)

links.outcome: Accuracy of fitness-for-surgery assessment with RAG grounding in guidelines vs non-RAG GPT-4
links.effect: GPT4_international RAG achieved 96.4% accuracy vs 92.9% for non-RAG GPT-4 and 92.9% for RAG with local guidelines; humans 86.6%.
links.quote: The Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT)4_international model emerged as the most accurate model with the highest accuracy in predicting medical fitness for surgery (96.4%) compared to answers given by human evaluators (86.6%), as well as its non-RAG counterpart (92.9%) and RAG counterpart with local guidelines (92.9%) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2 ).

links.outcome: Compare LLM-RAG accuracy against clinicians on same scenarios for surgical fitness
links.effect: GPT4_international outperformed human evaluators (96.4% vs 86.6%, OR 4.84, p=0.016); false negative rate 25% vs 62.5% for humans.
links.quote: The GPT4_international model performed better than humans in evaluations of patient’s fitness for surgery (Odds Ratio (OR) = 4.84, p = 0.016).

links.outcome: Reproducibility of GPT-4 international RAG outputs across repeated runs
links.effect: Reproducibility score 4.86/5 over 4 repeats; IRR 0.93 for fitness prediction, 0.96 for healthcare-team instructions, 0.92 for optimization types.
links.quote: The S.C.O.R.E (Safety, Consensus, Objectivity, Reproducibility, Explainability) evaluation showed that the GPT4 RAG model was able to have high reproducibility of results (4.86 out of 5) and provided safe instructions (4.93 out of 5) (Supplementary Table 7 ).

links.outcome: Hallucination/critical clinical error rates of LLMs and RAG versions
links.effect: Hallucination rates 0% to 2.9% for GPT3.5, GPT4, GPT4o, Llama3, Gemini, Claude; Llama2 much higher, RAG Llama2-7b 48.6% and 32.9% vs 12.8% native.
links.quote: Notably, the RAG-enhanced versions of the LLAMA2-7b model demonstrated substantially higher hallucination rates compared to their native counterparts, with rates of 48.6% and 32.9% versus 12.8%, respectively (Supplementary Table 4 ).

links.outcome: Accuracy in sicker ASA 3 patients across models in simulated scenarios
links.effect: GPT4 models had highest accuracy in ASA 3 patients, while Gemini and Llama2-13b had less than 50% accuracy.
links.quote: The comparison, the Gemini and Large Language Model Meta AI (LLAMA)2-13b models had less than 50% accuracy when assessing ASA 3 patients (Supplementary Fig 1 ).

openai.sample_unit: LLM- and human-generated response components to 14 clinical scenarios

links.effect: GPT4_international RAG accuracy 96.4% vs non-RAG GPT-4 92.9% and local-guideline RAG 92.9%.
links.quote: The Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT)4_international model emerged as the most accurate model with the highest accuracy in predicting medical fitness for surgery (96.4%) compared to answers given by human evaluators (86.6%), as well as its non-RAG counterpart (92.9%) and RAG counterpart with local guidelines (92.9%) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2 ).

links.effect: LLAMA2-7b RAG hallucinations 48.6% and 32.9% vs native 12.8%.
links.quote: Notably, the RAG-enhanced versions of the LLAMA2-7b model demonstrated substantially higher hallucination rates compared to their native counterparts, with rates of 48.6% and 32.9% versus 12.8%, respectively (Supplementary Table 4 ).

links.effect: Optimization 71.0% vs 55.0%, p=0.026; medication instructions 91.0% vs 98.0%, p=0.035.
links.quote: The secondary outcomes show that the GPT4_international model was better than humans at generating what medical optimization was required by the scenario (71.0% vs 55.0%, p = 0.026), but the human-generated answers were better than the GPT4_international model at generation of medication instructions order (91.0% vs 98.0%, p = 0.035) (Supplementary Table 4 and 5 ).

links.effect: Medically unfit classified fit: humans 62.5%, GPT4_international 25%.
links.quote: The false negative rate, which reflects instances where medically unfit patients were incorrectly identified as fit for surgery, was 62.5% among human evaluators compared to 25% in the GPT4_international model (Supplementary Table 8 ).

The S.C.O.R.E (Safety, Consensus, Objectivity, Reproducibility, Explainability) evaluation showed that the GPT4 RAG model was able to have high reproducibility of results (4.86 out of 5) and provided safe instructions (4.93 out of 5) (Supplementary Table 7 ).

links.outcome: accuracy in predicting medical fitness for surgery
links.effect: 96.4% for GPT4_international vs 92.9% for non-RAG counterpart, 92.9% for local RAG, and 86.6% for humans
links.quote: The Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT)4_international model emerged as the most accurate model with the highest accuracy in predicting medical fitness for surgery (96.4%) compared to answers given by human evaluators (86.6%), as well as its non-RAG counterpart (92.9%) and RAG counterpart with local guidelines (92.9%) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2 ).

links.outcome: hallucination rates of RAG-enhanced versus native models
links.effect: 48.6% and 32.9% for RAG-enhanced LLAMA2-7b versions versus 12.8% for native counterparts
links.quote: Notably, the RAG-enhanced versions of the LLAMA2-7b model demonstrated substantially higher hallucination rates compared to their native counterparts, with rates of 48.6% and 32.9% versus 12.8%, respectively (Supplementary Table 4 ).

screen.practice: retrieval grounding (RAG) with local and international guidelines
screen.reason: The study tests the implementation of retrieval augmented generation (RAG) using clinical guidelines to ground LLM outputs across clinical scenarios and compares performance to humans and base LLM responses.
